summary: Convivencia ('living together') was introduced as a historiographical concept by the Spanish historian Américo Castro in España en su historia (1948), to characterize the interaction of Christians, Muslims, and Jews in medieval Iberia as formative of Spanish culture and identity. It has since become one of the most contested framings in the history of medieval Iberia, championed, qualified, replaced, and rejected by historians who disagree about how coexistence, exchange, hierarchy, and violence among the three communities should be described.
description:
Américo Castro (1885-1972), a Spanish philologist and historian writing in exile in the United States, set out the thesis in España en su historia: cristianos, moros y judíos (Buenos Aires, 1948), reworked as La realidad histórica de España and in English as The Structure of Spanish History (1954). Kenneth Baxter Wolf, in a survey of the idea's history, dates the term's appearance as a historiographical concept to this controversial 1948 thesis about Spanish historical identity. Against accounts that traced a permanent Spanish character back to Roman and Visigothic Hispania, Castro argued that what became Spanish identity was formed in the medieval centuries through the convivencia of three 'castes', Christians, Moors, and Jews, and he developed the argument chiefly with reference to the Christian kingdoms, above all Castile, and to the cultural legacy that the Muslim and Jewish castes left within them. Scholars who later took up the term (Glick, Novikoff) stress that Castro's convivencia included tension and conflict and was not simply a synonym for tolerance. The medievalist Claudio Sánchez-Albornoz replied in España, un enigma histórico (1956), arguing for the continuity of a Hispanic character rooted before 711 and for the formative role of the Christian Reconquest, and assigning a much smaller role to Islamic and Jewish influence; the exchange between the two exiled scholars became one of the defining polemics of twentieth-century Spanish historiography.

Thomas Glick, in the volume Convivencia: Jews, Muslims, and Christians in Medieval Spain (1992), which accompanied an exhibition at the Jewish Museum in New York, used the term for patterns of interaction and cultural diffusion that included both exchange and friction, and Wolf credits such social-scientific models of acculturation with clarifying how cultural exchange worked and with tempering the tendency to romanticize convivencia. David Nirenberg's Communities of Violence (1996), a study of the fourteenth-century Crown of Aragon, argued that violence against Jews and Muslims was part of the structure of coexistence rather than its simple negation, and questioned the usefulness of the opposition between tolerance and intolerance for the Middle Ages. Brian Catlos, studying the Muslims of Aragon and Catalonia under Christian rule, proposed 'conveniencia' as an alternative model in which mutual interest, rather than tolerance, explained how communities lived together. Jonathan Ray (2005) likewise called for an approach to convivencia beyond the alternatives of tolerance and persecution, and Maya Soifer (2009) argued that the concept had become more an impediment than a help to the study of Christian Spain, that the evidence for Islamic influence on interfaith coexistence there is scarce, and that the polarization between 'tolerance' and 'persecution' neglects the power relations among Jews, Christians, and Muslims. On the wider comparison of Jewish life under Islam and under Christendom, Mark R. Cohen (1994) described two opposed myths, an 'interfaith utopia' under Islam and a 'neo-lachrymose' picture of unrelieved persecution, and rejected both.

In wider public discussion the term has often been extended to al-Andalus and associated with tolerance. María Rosa Menocal's The Ornament of the World (2002), a widely read book, presented al-Andalus as a 'culture of tolerance'; Wolf and Soifer, among others, have criticized romanticized uses of the concept (Soifer with reference to Christian Spain). Darío Fernández-Morera's The Myth of the Andalusian Paradise (2016) argued that the image of a tolerant al-Andalus is a myth and emphasized religious hierarchy and violence under Islamic rule; S. J. Pearce responded that Fernández-Morera's book itself exemplifies the use of medieval Spain as a proxy in contemporary political debate. Alex Novikoff's historiographical survey (2005) traces the oscillation between tolerant and intolerant readings of medieval Spain from Castro and Sánchez-Albornoz onward and treats that oscillation as itself an enigma of the historiography.
editorial_notes: HOME TRADITION (ADR-0010): this concept is filed under christianity. The entity concerns all three communities, and the editor judged the choice genuinely unclear, so the reason is given here. Castro introduced and applied the concept chiefly to the Christian kingdoms of medieval Spain and to the formation of the identity of Christian Spain, the founding polemic (Castro against Sánchez-Albornoz) concerned that national history, and much of the scholarship that refined the term (Nirenberg on the Crown of Aragon, Catlos on Muslims under Christian rule, Soifer on interfaith relations in Christian Spain) studies minorities within Christian polities. An alternative reading is acknowledged: because that scholarship is chiefly about Jewish and Muslim minorities, and because popular usage (Menocal, and in critique Fernández-Morera) attaches the term to al-Andalus, a case could be made for filing it under judaism or islam. The editor judged christianity the more accurate home for the concept as introduced, and the entry links to al-andalus and to the Jewish and Muslim entries it concerns. The home is a storage convention, not a claim of ownership. NEUTRALITY: the entry presents convivencia strictly as a contested historiographical framing; it records the concept and its critics and defenders, attributes each characterization to its proponent, and takes no position on whether convivencia 'really' existed or on how much tolerance, exchange, hierarchy, or violence characterized medieval Iberia (principles #1 and #2). The popular poles are both cited only as attributed positions and both are set against scholarly criticism: Menocal's championing alongside the criticism of romanticized uses of the concept by Wolf and Soifer, among others (Soifer with reference to Christian Spain), and Fernández-Morera's critique alongside Pearce's response; neither the 'golden age' nor the 'myth' reading is endorsed. Authors are introduced without credentials so that no position is privileged by them. SOURCING (principles #8 and #9): for a modern historiographical concept the primary texts are the historians' own works, here Castro (1948; English 1954) and Sánchez-Albornoz (1956). The scholarly debate is represented by Glick (in Mann, Glick, and Dodds, eds., 1992, a volume produced with the Jewish Museum, New York), Cohen (1994), Nirenberg (1996), Catlos (2004), Novikoff (2005), Ray (2005, in Jewish Social Studies), Wolf (2009), Soifer (2009), and Pearce (2020); the popular poles by Menocal (2002) and Fernández-Morera (2016). Jewish-studies vantages are present (Cohen, Ray, the Jewish Museum volume). No modern Muslim scholarly treatment of the term itself was verified for this entry; Jayyusi's The Legacy of Muslim Spain was considered but was not verified to treat convivencia as a concept, so it is not cited here. A reported claim that the word derives from Ramón Menéndez Pidal's linguistic usage could not be verified and is not made. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited. CONFIDENCE: all sources were verified to exist and to be on-topic through publisher pages, library catalogues, DOIs, and published reviews or abstracts (Catlos's conveniencia model as set against Castro's convivencia is confirmed by a published review of the 2004 book; Wolf's and Soifer's positions are taken from their published abstracts, the full texts not being openly accessible); none was read line by line, so confidence is medium throughout. The historical_period start marks Castro's 1948 introduction of the concept; the term refers to medieval Iberia from the eighth century to the end of the fifteenth and, in some usage, to the Morisco period.

historical_period.note: The term was introduced by Américo Castro in España en su historia (1948) and remains in active scholarly and public use, so no end is given. It refers to the medieval Iberian peninsula from the conquest of 711 to the end of the fifteenth century and, in some usage, to the Mudejar and Morisco centuries that followed.

relations.note: Although Castro developed the term chiefly for the Christian kingdoms, later scholarly and popular usage extended it to Muslim-ruled al-Andalus, whose characterization is one of the most disputed questions in the debate.

The conquest of 711 brought Muslims, Christians, and Jews into the configuration of communities that the convivencia debate addresses; Castro and Sánchez-Albornoz disagreed sharply over its significance for Spanish history.

Under Muslim rule in al-Andalus, Jews and Christians held the protected status that Islamic law grounded in their classification as People of the Book; how that status should be characterized is part of the debate.

The coerced Christian-Jewish disputation held before James I of Aragon in 1263 is an instance of interreligious relations in a Christian Iberian kingdom of the kind the debate over convivencia concerns.
The end of the last Muslim polity in Iberia in 1492 is commonly treated in the debate as a closing point of medieval coexistence.

The expulsion of the Jews from Castile and Aragon in 1492 is commonly treated in the debate as a closing point of medieval coexistence, and historians differ over how it relates to earlier patterns of coexistence and violence.
The forcibly converted Muslims of sixteenth-century Spain and their descendants are included by some historians in the later history of coexistence and its end.
The expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609-1614 is treated by some historians as the final end of the coexistence of the three communities in Iberia.
